newsitem.title: INDIA: After polls, Kashmir seeks stable India government.
newsitem.headline: After polls, Kashmir seeks stable India government.

text.p: Kashmiri politicians will return to their jobs after six years next month but they said that the real success of the state's key local polls this month would depend on a stable Indian government.

Simmering turbulence in New Delhi over a key assembly poll in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh next month and a change in the leadership of the Congress party which supports the ruling alliance would have a bearing on Kashmir, they said.

"Kashmir will need the caring hand of New Delhi, more than ever after these elections," Wasim Ahmed, general secretary of Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party, told Reuters on Sunday.
India poured in tens of thousands of paramilitary forces to conduct a violence-marked election for the Jammu and Kashmir state assembly this month, the first in nine years.
"It is in India's national interest and all its politicians that Kashmir is not ignored in the hurly burly of partisan politics in New Delhi," Ahmed said.
At least 21 people have been killed in the month-long campaign in which several candidates survived assassination attempts by separatist militants who oppose the polls.

Former Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah's National Conference is widely expected to win a majority in the 87-seat assembly but his Congress party rivals contest the claim saying the next government would be theirs.
Abdullah's party has had an uneasy relationship with the Congress, accusing it of engineering defections to topple his government in the past.

But Abdullah is also known to have friends in the Congress party who want to forge closer ties with his National Conference than was possible with former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao as Congress chief.
Rao resigned as Congress president on Saturday after a New Delhi court ordered him to face charges in a cheating case.
"We are naturally looking eagerly at the developments," a National Conference politician said. "The changes could affect the situation in Kashmir in many ways, directly and indirectly."

Indian officials, handling Kashmir for six years after New Delhi dissolved the state assembly at the start of a separatist uprising, said an unstable government in the Indian capital would adversely affect their campaign against separatist militants.

"How much time does New Delhi have for Kashmir?" a senior security official in charge of anti-guerrilla operations asked. "By all accounts this is the most sensitive part of the country. It needs special handling by a confident government in Delhi."
Abdullah told a rally last week he would fight for more autonomy for Kashmir after the polls, telling New Delhi: "Kashmir is the crown of India, please don't wear it around your feet."
The powerful Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) says it would block any move for extra privileges for Kashmir, Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state.
The BJP is the largest party in Uttar Pradesh where Deve Gowda's United Front and the Congress party have mounted a challenge to its supremacy but in separate campaigns.
A BJP victory in Uttar Pradesh could spur the party to jockey for early parliamentary polls, its leaders say.
Campaigning in Uttar Pradesh recently, Rao, too held out a veiled threat against Deve Gowda.
"We are supporting the government in New Delhi to keep the BJP out," he told a rally.
Deve Gowda is seen as sympathetic to Abdullah's National Conference party. Ahmed said the Janata Dal could even join Abdullah's government.
"In some ways Kashmir is not dissimilar to the rest of India," he said. "Ideally, all the forces opposed to the BJP should have a common destiny in Kashmir as in the rest India."
